claims.text: Rate-limited dislocation climb governs high-temperature plastic strain in polycrystalline tungsten alloys intended for fusion plasma-facing components.
Rate-limited dislocation climb governs high-temperature toughness in polycrystalline tungsten alloys intended for fusion plasma-facing components.
The spacing and distribution of nanoscale carbide precipitates modulate dislocation-climb-controlled deformation.
Controlled alloying and heat treatment can introduce and engineer nanoscale carbide precipitate spacing and distributions in the tungsten alloy.
Nanoscale carbide precipitates interact with and impede dislocation networks.
Dislocation climb is the dominant plasticity mechanism in the stated high-temperature regime.
Carbide precipitates act as obstacles that slow dislocation climb.
Slower dislocation climb reduces the overall rate of plastic deformation.
An optimized precipitate spacing will produce lower creep rates than the baseline tungsten alloy.
An optimized precipitate spacing will improve toughness relative to the baseline tungsten alloy.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to polycrystalline tungsten alloys under mechanical testing at 1200–1800 K.
Secondary deformation mechanisms may affect the observed high-temperature behavior.
Radiation damage may affect the observed behavior.
The proposed comparison uses precipitate-modified and baseline samples tested at 1200–1800 K under otherwise identical controlled stress conditions.
Failure to observe both lower creep rates and enhanced toughness, or failure to observe altered dislocation-climb behavior by TEM, is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.
